slides: In this optional lesson, let's see why the Pythagorean theorem works.

slides.say: As I said, you don't need this for the exam. You won't be asked to prove the theorem. This is a short extra lesson, if you're curious: what the theorem says about areas, and a simple proof. If you prefer, you can skip to the next video.

First, what does a squared look like? It's the area of the square whose side is a. So let's put one square on leg a. Its area is a squared. In the same way, a square on leg b has area b squared, and a square on the hypotenuse c has area c squared.
at: So let's put one square on leg a
a square on the hypotenuse c

slides.say: So the theorem says that the two squares on the legs together have exactly the same area as the square on the hypotenuse. With legs three and four and hypotenuse five, nine plus sixteen is twenty-five.

Now let's see why. Take a big square, and put four copies of our right triangle in its corners. Their hypotenuses make one tilted shape in the middle. Is that shape really square? Its four sides are all c, the hypotenuses. Each corner of the middle shape sits between two acute angles of the triangles. Those two angles add up to ninety degrees. Together with the middle corner, they make a straight angle of a hundred eighty. So the middle corner is ninety degrees too. The uncovered shape is a square with side c and area c squared.

Now take the same big square, and move the same four triangles into new places, two at the top right and two at the bottom left. The pieces haven't changed: the same four triangles, with the same legs a and b. Now the part they don't cover is one square with side a and one square with side b.
at: Now take the same big square
Now the part they don't cover

slides: The big square didn't change, and the four triangles didn't change. So the part they leave uncovered has the same area both times. a squared plus b squared equals c squared. That's the picture. Now let's write it with areas.

slides.say: Look at the first picture again. The big square is made of the middle square, c squared, and four triangles around it. Each one is a right triangle, so its area is leg times leg over two, which is a b over two.
at: Look at the first picture again

slides.say: But the big square also has its own area formula, side times side. Its side is a plus b, so its area is the bracket a plus b, squared.
at: Its side is a plus b

slides.say: Both describe the same area, so they're equal. Using the square-of-a-sum formula we learned, a plus b, squared, is a squared, plus two a b, plus b squared.

On the other side, four times a b over two is two a b. Two a b is on both sides, so it cancels, and we're left with a squared plus b squared equals c squared. That's the theorem, and it was simpler than you thought. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
